issues.legal_issue: An order determining possession in summary proceedings before an Executive Magistrate does not bind a competent court’s final adjudication of the parties’ civil rights.
material_facts: The Magistrate attached the disputed shop and, after proceedings in which the respondent was not given an opportunity to participate, declared the appellant to be in possession.
The respondent later brought a title-based civil suit concerning the shop.
The Magistrate’s order followed a summary inquiry into possession, rather than an adjudication of title or civil rights.
issues.conclusion: A competent court may determine possession and entitlement to possession independently of the Magistrate’s finding; at final adjudication, that finding is only one piece of evidence and does not bind the competent court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 145(4), 145(6) and 146(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Magistrate’s inquiry concerns possession and preserves the position pending determination by a court competent to decide civil rights. A competent court means a court with jurisdiction to determine title, rights, or entitlement to possession, and need not necessarily be a civil court. The Magistrate’s order is relevant as evidence of the order made and, between the parties, of possession, but its reasoning and findings do not bind the competent court. The Court relied on Bhinka v. Charan Singh, AIR 1959 SC 960, and Jhunamal alias Devandas v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (1988) 4 SCC 452, and also referred to Anil Behari Ghosh v. Smt. Latika Bala Dassi, AIR 1955 SC 566, on the limited evidentiary relevance of a criminal court judgment.

predicates.subsequent_competent_proceeding: A proceeding is brought before a court with jurisdiction to determine the parties’ rights or entitlement to possession after a summary possession order has been made.
predicates.magistrate_made_summary_possession_order: An Executive Magistrate made an order about possession after a summary inquiry into a dispute likely to cause a breach of the peace.
predicates.court_finally_adjudicates_entitlement: The competent court makes a final adjudication of the parties’ rights or entitlement to possession on the evidence before it.

issues.definition: When a competent court finally adjudicates entitlement after a summary possession order, it may make its own finding on possession.

issues.legal_issue: A competent court may exceptionally grant an interlocutory injunction or other interim arrangement inconsistent with an Executive Magistrate’s possession order.
material_facts: The Magistrate’s order declared the appellant to be in possession, although the respondent claimed possession and had sought to participate in the proceedings but was not heard.
The person originally proceeded against by the Magistrate disclaimed an interest in the shop and did not contest the proceedings.
In the title-based civil suit, the Civil Judge restrained the appellant from interfering with the respondent’s possession and directed that she be put in possession.
The District Judge set aside that interim order because it conflicted with the Magistrate’s order, while the High Court restored it.
issues.conclusion: The competent court has jurisdiction to make an interim order inconsistent with the Magistrate’s order, but should do so only exceptionally, on a strong prima facie case and after recording its reasons and satisfaction. The Court dismissed the appeal from the High Court’s order restoring the Civil Judge’s interim order.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an interim injunction depends on a prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury. A court should ordinarily respect an order made by the Executive Magistrate under Sections 145 or 146 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and should be cautious about making an inconsistent interim arrangement. That caution does not remove the court’s jurisdiction: departure may be justified exceptionally where material shows a strong prima facie case that the Magistrate’s findings are without jurisdiction, palpably wrong, or self-contradictory, or that continuing the arrangement would be unjust or inequitable. The court must record its reasons and satisfaction.

rule.if: civil_proceeding_after_magistrate_order and interlocutory_relief_sought and strong_prima_facie_basis_to_depart and court_records_reasons

predicates.civil_proceeding_after_magistrate_order: A civil proceeding is brought after an Executive Magistrate has made an order concerning possession of the disputed property.
predicates.interlocutory_relief_sought: A party asks the court for an interim injunction or other interim arrangement concerning possession of the property.
predicates.strong_prima_facie_basis_to_depart: Material before the court strongly supports departing from the Magistrate’s arrangement, such as because the order appears without jurisdiction, palpably wrong, self-contradictory, or unjust to maintain.
predicates.court_records_reasons: The court records its reasons and satisfaction for making an interim arrangement that departs from the Magistrate’s order.

issues.definition: When interim relief is sought after a Magistrate’s possession order, a court may grant inconsistent relief if a strong prima facie basis to depart exists and the court records its reasons.

issues.legal_issue: A party seeking adjudication of rights to property attached by an Executive Magistrate need not also seek recovery of possession where the property is held in custody of the law.
material_facts: The Magistrate ordered the disputed shop attached as a case of emergency.
The attachment placed the property in the Magistrate’s custody pending determination of the parties’ rights by a competent court.
issues.conclusion: Where the property is attached and held in custody of the law, it is sufficient for the party seeking relief to ask the competent court to determine the rights concerning entitlement to possession; a separate prayer for recovery of possession is not necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Section 146(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for attachment pending determination of the parties’ rights by a competent court. Because attached property is held in custody of the law for the party who ultimately establishes entitlement to possession, a proceeding seeking determination of that entitlement need not include a separate claim for recovery of possession.

predicates.proceeding_after_property_attachment: A proceeding is brought before a competent court after the disputed property has been attached by an Executive Magistrate.
predicates.property_held_in_legal_custody: The attached property remains in the custody of the law pending determination of the parties’ rights.
predicates.party_seeks_determination_of_possession_: A party asks the competent court to determine who is entitled to possession of the attached property.

issues.definition: If attached property remains in legal custody and a party seeks determination of possession rights, that determination may be sought without a separate claim for recovery of possession.
